title: Kitt Peak and a Northern Asterism
caption: The Big Dipper over Kitt Peak National Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: On the left stands the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, and on the right the UA Bok 2.3-meter Telescope, both at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). High in the sky to the right, above the Mayall, are the stars of the Big Dipper, and a faint glow hangs over the Bok telescope. The mountain hosts twenty optical and two radio telescopes, one of the largest gatherings of astronomical instruments in the northern hemisphere.

The Big Dipper is an asterism, a recognisable pattern within the larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. Its stars are circumpolar. They sit so close to the north celestial pole that at most northern latitudes they never set. They stay above the horizon in daytime too, hidden only by the far brighter sunlight.
The glow over the Bok telescope is the Gegenschein. It is sunlight reflected by interplanetary dust in the part of the sky opposite the Sun.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Tomáš Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the faint Gegenschein would be much harder to see in person.

explore: The photograph was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. The photographer, Tomáš Slovinský, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador. The picture appeared as a NOIRLab Image of the Week.
alt: Two telescopes at Kitt Peak under a night sky, with the Big Dipper high at right and a faint glow above the right-hand telescope.
